newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Analysts puzzled by CITIC Pacific deal.
newsitem.headline: Analysts puzzled by CITIC Pacific deal.

text.p: News that a CITIC Pacific Ltd management team would buy a 15.47 percent stake in the company from parent China International Trust & Investment Corp Hong Kong (Holdings) Ltd left many analysts puzzled on Monday.
"It's curious," Philip Tulks at DBS Securities said.
"It's not known what the company wants," said Herbert Lau of Vickers Ballas Hong Kong.
But the immediate market reponse was overwhelmingly positive as CITIC Pacific shares surged 6.4 percent to a record high of HK$46.40 before closing Monday's session at HK$45.60.
Brokers said the move by the management team, headed by chairman Larry Yung, showed their confidence in the company and that downside in the share price should be very limited.
But analysts said the stock was overbought fundamentally and technically.
"Today's rise is unreasonable and the deal should not affect (benefit) small shareholders," one analyst said.

Shares of CITIC Pacific, a diversified group with interests ranging from trading and distribution to property investment and aviation, were trading at an historical price-earnings multiple of 28.57 times.
CITIC Hong Kong, a unit of China's state trading giant China International Trust & Investment Corp, would hold 26.45 percent of CITIC Pacific after the deal from the current 41.92 percent.

CITIC Pacific also said on Monday that Yung had lifted his stake by 291 million shares or 13.64 percent of its issued share capital and that managing director Henry Fan had increased his holding by 30 million shares or about 1.41 percent.
Yung's interest in the company was 103.18 million shares and Fan's was 13 million shares as of June 30, 1996, its interim report showed.
Lau said there was a possibility the parent would use the proceeds to invest in its Chinese projects and later inject the investments into CITIC Pacific by having it issue new shares to the parent.
"It looks like an internal financing arrangement," Lau said, adding that the move, unlike placements which flood the market with shares, would not depress CITIC Pacific's share price.

"But fundamentally it doesn't change, in particular because there have been no new shares issued and thus no earnings dilution," Tulk said. "It does put the company more directly in the hands of its management."
Analysts said the discount given to the management team was on the large side as the price of HK$33 a share was about 24 percent below Friday's close of HK$43.60.
"The minority shareholders have got to be wondering what the hell's going on," Tulk said.
Some analysts speculated the discount was a way of keeping managment in their seats in the sensitive period before Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30 next year.
CITIC Pacific might also fear losing its edge as a red chip, or Chinese-controlled but Hong Kong-based company, if CITIC Hong Kong places shares to shareholders outside China, Tulk said.
